content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a chronic genetic condition characterized by hemolysis and inflammation. Individuals with SCD often experience increased metabolic demands and reduced energy and nutrient intake, leading to deficiencies in both macronutrients and micronutrients, including vitamin D. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation in children and adults with SCD, comparing different dosing regimens and assessing its impact on general health, musculoskeletal health, respiratory health, and safety. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving 39 participants compared oral vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) supplementation (20 participants) to placebo (19 participants) over six weeks. Only 25 participants completed the six-month follow-up. The study demonstrated a high risk of bias due to incomplete outcome data but had low risk for randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and selective outcome reporting. Vitamin D supplementation likely increased serum 25(OH)D levels at eight weeks (mean difference [MD] 29.79 nmol/L), 16 weeks (MD 12.67 nmol/L), and 24 weeks (MD 15.52 nmol/L), based on moderate-quality evidence. Adverse events, such as tingling of the lips or hands, were rare and showed little difference between the vitamin D and placebo groups (low-quality evidence). Vitamin D supplementation may have reduced the number of pain days at eight weeks (MD -10.00 days), but it was associated with a lower health-related quality of life score in physical functioning at 16 weeks (MD -12.56) and 24 weeks (MD -12.59), although this effect was not observed at eight weeks (low-quality evidence). Two additional RCTs (83 participants) compared different vitamin D dosing regimens. One study (62 participants) compared daily doses of 7000 IU and 4000 IU of vitamin D3 over 12 weeks, while the other study (21 participants) compared monthly doses of 100,000 IU and 12,000 IU of vitamin D3 over 24 months. Both studies had low risk of bias for blinding and incomplete outcome data, but one study had a high risk of selective outcome reporting bias. The higher monthly dose of 100,000 IU may have resulted in greater increases in serum 25(OH)D levels at one year (MD 16.40 nmol/L) and two years (MD 18.96 nmol/L), based on low-quality evidence. Adverse events were similar between the two dosing groups (low-quality evidence). However, the higher dose group experienced more episodes of acute chest syndrome at one year (MD 0.27 episodes), though this difference was not observed at two years (MD 0.09 episodes). Pain levels and forced expiratory volume in one second (% predicted) showed little or no difference between the dosing groups at one and two years (moderate-quality evidence). However, the higher dose group had lower % predicted forced vital capacity at both one year (MD -7.20%) and two years (MD -7.10%). Muscle health, assessed in both hands, showed no significant differences between the dosing regimens. The study comparing daily doses of 7000 IU and 4000 IU did not provide sufficient data for analysis, but median serum 25(OH)D levels were reported to be lower in the lower-dose group at six and 12 weeks. Additionally, median serum parathyroid hormone levels were lower in the higher-dose group at 12 weeks. The authors concluded that the current evidence from these three RCTs is of insufficient quality to inform clinical practice. Until more robust evidence becomes available, clinicians should adhere to existing guidelines for vitamin D supplementation and dietary reference intakes for calcium and vitamin D. Well-designed, parallel-group RCTs are needed to evaluate the effects and safety of vitamin D supplementation and to determine the optimal dosing regimens for children and adults with SCD.
